relationship: Same-chapter Simeonite lot and stated reason for its position
rationale: The second lot lies within Judah's lots; the closing explanation repeats that arrangement and grounds it in Judah's larger portion.

relationship: Beer-sheba named in the Judah and Simeon catalogues
rationale: Beer-sheba occurs in both town lists, while the Simeon heading expressly places its inheritance amid Judah's lots; the other names remain unchanged.

relationship: Shared Asom entry within related tribal catalogues
rationale: Asom is named in both the Judah and Simeon lists; Arsola and Bola are not equated with Judah's other names.

relationship: Shared Hormah entry within related tribal catalogues
rationale: Hormah appears among both Judah's cities and Simeon's towns, consistent with the stated nested lots without identifying the differently named neighbouring entries.

relationship: Shared Ziklag entry in the nested lot descriptions
rationale: Both lists name Ziklag, while the surrounding towns have different supplied forms and Simeon's inheritance is explicitly situated within Judah's lot.

relationship: Same-chapter thirteen-city group and its preceding named entries
rationale: Batharoth closes the group counted as thirteen cities, following Beer-sheba through Sarsousin in the preceding four units; villages and fields remain separately stated.

relationship: Same-chapter four-city group and Simeonite territorial closure
rationale: Eremmon, Thalcha, Ether and Ashan form the stated four-city group before the surrounding extent toward Barek and Bameth closes Simeon's divisional inheritance.

relationship: Same-chapter Simeonite boundary closure and lot heading
rationale: The extent toward Barek and Bameth closes the Simeonite inheritance introduced as the second lot amid Judah, preserving the named southwestern endpoint.

relationship: Same-chapter explanation of the nested Judah-Simeon allocation
rationale: The explanation that Judah's portion was larger accounts for the heading's statement that Simeon's inheritance lay among Judah's lots.

relationship: Same-chapter Zebulun lot heading and allocation summary
rationale: The third lot names Zebulun and begins at Esedek; the summary identifies the enclosed cities and villages as Zebulun's divisional inheritance.

relationship: Same-chapter specified boundary segment within Zebulun's allocation
rationale: Gola, the sea and Maragella borders, and the ravine facing Jekman belong to the account closed as Zebulun's city-and-village inheritance, without assigning Maragella a modern coastal identity.

relationship: Same-chapter eastern boundary places and enclosing tribal allocation
rationale: The eastward route through Seddouk, Bethsamys, Chaselothaith, Daberoth and Phangai falls within the description concluded as Zebulun's inheritance, without modern place identifications.

relationship: Same-chapter named eastern route within Zebulun's inheritance
rationale: Gebere, Katasem, Remmona, Amathar and Aoza are named on the eastern turn of the border account assigned in its closure to Zebulun.

relationship: Same-chapter contrasting eastern and northern boundary turns
rationale: The preceding route turns east through named places; this unit turns the boundary north toward Amoth and specifies Gaiphael as the endpoint.

relationship: Same-chapter named city group and tribal summary
rationale: Katanath, Nabaal, Symoon, Jericho and Bethman precede the explicit Zebulun city-and-village summary; the Jericho name is not assigned an outside site identity.

relationship: Same-chapter Zebulun allocation closure and third-lot introduction
rationale: The city-and-village summary closes the inheritance introduced as Zebulun's third lot, tying the enclosed route to that stated tribal division.

relationship: Same-chapter Issachar fourth-lot heading and closure
rationale: The fourth lot is assigned to Issachar, and the concluding statement identifies its enclosed towns and villages as that tribe's divisional inheritance.

relationship: Same-chapter Jazel group within the Issachar allotment
rationale: Jazel, Chasaloth and Shunem open the named border list closed by the explicit Issachar cities-and-villages allocation, without imposing another edition's town forms.

relationship: Same-chapter named Issachar town group and allocation summary
rationale: Agin, Siona, Reeroth and Anachereth stand within the fourth-lot list whose closure identifies Issachar as the recipient of these cities and villages.

relationship: Kison named in Issachar's allotment and Levitical contribution
rationale: Kison occurs in Issachar's border list and among the cities supplied from Issachar to Gershon's Levites; Dabiron and Rebes are not renamed.

relationship: Same-chapter named Issachar group within its tribal closure
rationale: Remmas, Jeon, Tomman, Aimarek and Bersaphes belong to the city account explicitly closed as Issachar's inheritance; similar names elsewhere are not identified as equivalents.

relationship: Same-chapter Jordan endpoint and Issachar allocation closure
rationale: The border passing Gaithbor, Salim and Bethsamys ends at Jordan, immediately before the declaration that these cities and villages form Issachar's inheritance.

relationship: Same-chapter Issachar inheritance closure and fourth-lot heading
rationale: The statement assigning the cities and villages to Issachar closes the section introduced by its fourth lot, preserving the stated tribal recipient.

relationship: Same-chapter Asher fifth-lot heading and allocation summary
rationale: Asher receives the fifth lot, and the closing formula identifies the intervening borders, cities and villages as its divisional inheritance.

relationship: Same-chapter opening Asher border names and tribal closure
rationale: Eleketh, Aleph, Baithok and Keaph begin the border account concluded as Asher's city-and-village inheritance; no similarly spelled outside places are substituted.

relationship: Same-chapter Carmel-side border within Asher's inheritance
rationale: Elimelech, Amiel and Maasa lead toward Carmel, Sion and Labanath within the section closed as Asher's allocation, retaining each supplied geographical form.

relationship: Same-chapter boundary meeting a separately described tribal inheritance
rationale: Asher's boundary explicitly joins Zebulun, whose city-and-village inheritance has already been closed; the named Gai and Phtaiel route is preserved without site harmonization.

relationship: Asher and Sidon in allocation and incomplete-occupation accounts
rationale: Sidon the Great occurs in Asher's boundary; Judges later names Sidon among inhabitants Asher did not remove, preserving the difference between allocation and possession.

relationship: Same-chapter seaward boundary and Asher allocation summary
rationale: The route through Ramah, Masphassat and the Tyrians ends at the sea within the border section assigned to Asher, preserving Jasiph, Leb and Echozob.

relationship: Same-chapter final named Asher town group and tribal recipient
rationale: Archob, Aphek and Raau finish the named list before the explicit assignment of cities and villages to Asher, without equating Raau with another name.

relationship: Same-chapter Asher allocation closure and fifth-lot introduction
rationale: The city-and-village summary closes the portion introduced by Asher's fifth lot, identifying the recipient of the enclosed boundary description.

relationship: Same-chapter Naphtali sixth-lot heading and inheritance closure
rationale: Naphtali receives the sixth lot, and the closing statement identifies the intervening boundary and city descriptions as that tribe's inheritance.

relationship: Same-chapter Jordan endpoint and subsequent directional description
rationale: The named route ends at Jordan; the next description again places Jordan toward sunrise while locating Zebulun south and Asher seaward, preserving the distinct directional statements.

relationship: Same-chapter overlapping named tribal neighbours
rationale: Naphtali's border names Zebulun and Asher as neighbours; Asher's own earlier border explicitly joins Zebulun, without requiring identical town names or modern boundary reconstruction.

relationship: Same-chapter walled-city subgroup within the Naphtali section
rationale: Tyre, Omatha, Daketh and Chinnereth appear as the Tyrians' walled-city group inside the section closed as Naphtali's inheritance; both descriptions remain intact.

relationship: Same-chapter named city group and tribal closure
rationale: Armaith, Arael and Hazor occur within the city sequence closed as Naphtali's inheritance, without identifying them with similarly named towns in other allotments.

relationship: Kedesh in Naphtali's list and the refuge appointment
rationale: Kedesh occurs within Naphtali's city list; the refuge appointment explicitly identifies Kedesh in Galilee in Naphtali's mountain, without transferring the other listed towns' roles.

relationship: Same-chapter final Naphtali city group and allocation conclusion
rationale: Keroe, Megala, Arim, Beththame and Thessamys precede the explicit Naphtali inheritance closure; the unusual supplied names are not replaced by outside equivalents.

relationship: Same-chapter Naphtali inheritance closure and sixth-lot heading
rationale: The declaration of Naphtali's inheritance closes the section introduced as the sixth lot, connecting its particular borders and city groups to that tribe.

relationship: Same-chapter Dan seventh-lot heading and city summary
rationale: Dan receives the seventh lot, and the section's city-and-village summary identifies the inheritance of its divisions before the additional occupation accounts.

relationship: Same-chapter initial Dan border group and tribal allocation
rationale: Sarath, Asa and the cities of Sammaus begin the border account closed as Dan's divisional city-and-village inheritance, preserving their actual supplied forms.

relationship: Same-chapter Salabin group within Dan's inheritance
rationale: Salabin, Ammon and Silatha are included in the named Dan sequence whose closure assigns its cities and villages to that tribe.

relationship: Ekron recurring in distinct tribal allotment lists
rationale: Ekron appears in both the Dan city list and Judah's city-and-village catalogue; the different stated allocations remain recorded without resolving their territorial overlap.

relationship: Same-chapter named Dan town group and tribal summary
rationale: Alkatha, Begethon and Gebeelan stand within the seventh-lot sequence closed as Dan's city-and-village inheritance, without importing differently spelled identifications.

relationship: Gath-rimmon in Dan's inheritance and Levitical contribution
rationale: Gath-rimmon is named in Dan's border list and among the four cities supplied from Dan to the remaining Kohathites, preserving the separate allocation roles.

relationship: Same-chapter Joppa-side boundary and Dan inheritance closure
rationale: The sea-side Jerakon boundary near Joppa closes the route immediately before Dan's cities-and-villages summary; no modern coastline identification is added.

relationship: Same-chapter Dan inheritance summary and seventh-lot heading
rationale: The city-and-village allocation closes Dan's seventh-lot account, keeping that formal allotment distinct from the following account of Amorite pressure.

relationship: Closely parallel Amorite pressure upon Dan
rationale: Both state that Amorites pressed Dan into the hill country and prevented descent into the valley, preserving this continuation unit's placement in Joshua.

relationship: Judah's Lachish capture and its named city catalogue
rationale: Lachish is named among Judah's towns and here in a capture attributed to Judah; the new name Lasendak and the stated actors are retained without substitution.

relationship: Amorite persistence and tribute with distinct names and recipients
rationale: Both describe remaining Amorites brought under tribute by a heavy hand; Joshua names Ephraim, Elom and Salamin, while Judges names Joseph's house and a different mountain description.

relationship: Joshua's grant repeated in a separate continuation
rationale: Both record Israel giving Joshua a portion among them; the later continuation specifies the commanded grant and the requested city of Thamnasarach.

relationship: Repeated requested-city grant
rationale: Both state that Joshua received the city he requested by divine command and name Thamnasarach in Ephraim's mountain, preserving the actual city form.

relationship: Repeated building and residence of Joshua
rationale: The statement that Joshua built the granted city and lived there is repeated in the separate continuation immediately following the Thamnasarach grant.

relationship: Repeated leaders and lot-based inheritance distribution
rationale: Both name Eleazar, Joshua and ancestral leaders as distributors of the inheritance and describe allotment by divine instruction, with this closure additionally specifying Shiloh and the tent doors.

relationship: Shiloh casting of lots and distribution closure
rationale: The closure locates the inheritance lots at Shiloh before the Lord; the earlier account explicitly records Joshua casting the lots there before the Lord.

relationship: Divine refuge instruction addressed through successive leaders
rationale: Joshua receives a divine speech introducing refuge appointments; Numbers records the Lord's earlier command to Moses to provide such towns when Israel crosses into Canaan.

relationship: Explicit reference to the Mosaic refuge command
rationale: Joshua is told to appoint the refuges previously commanded through Moses; Numbers specifies their purpose and the six-town division across Jordan and in Canaan.

relationship: Unintentional killing and protection pending communal judgment
rationale: Both provide refuge for the involuntary killer against the blood avenger until the person stands before the congregation for judgment, retaining the actual stated protection.

relationship: Hebron named both refuge and Aaronic city
rationale: Hebron is appointed as the western refuge in Judah and separately given to Aaron's sons expressly as a refuge city with allotted lands.

relationship: Eastern three-town refuge list with distinct place forms
rationale: Both appoint refuges to Reuben's plain, Gad's Gilead and Manasseh's Bashan; Bosor/Aremoth/Gaulon and Bezer/Ramoth/Golan remain in their original forms without independent identity verification.

relationship: Refuge access for Israel and attached foreigners
rationale: Both expressly include Israelites and resident foreigners within the refuge provision for unintentional killing; Joshua additionally restates protection until congregational judgment.

relationship: Same distribution leadership approached by the Levites
rationale: Levitical ancestral heads approach Eleazar, Joshua and tribal heads, the same named offices previously identified as distributing Israel's inheritance, preserving their distinct petitioner and distributor roles.

relationship: Levitical petition cites the town-and-pasture command
rationale: The Levites request dwelling cities and surrounding lands for livestock through Moses' command; Numbers expressly directs Israel to supply towns and livestock lands from their possessions.

relationship: Narrated giving of Levitical cities follows the instruction
rationale: Israel gives cities and surrounding lands when assigning inheritance, corresponding to the earlier command to provide those Levitical dwelling towns from the allotted possessions.

relationship: Same-chapter Aaronic thirteen-city allotment and total
rationale: The lot assigns Aaron's Kohathite priests thirteen cities from Judah, Simeon and Benjamin; the later Aaronic summary repeats the thirteen-city total.

relationship: Same-chapter remaining Kohathite ten-city allocation and total
rationale: The allocation names Ephraim, Dan and half-Manasseh as contributors; its closing statement totals ten cities for these remaining Kohathite divisions.

relationship: Same-chapter Gershonite thirteen-city allocation and total
rationale: Gershon receives thirteen cities from the four named tribal portions, and the Gershonite closure repeats the thirteen-city total for its divisions.

relationship: Same-chapter Merarite twelve-city allocation and total
rationale: The lot assigns Merari twelve cities from Reuben, Gad and Zebulun; the later Merarite closure repeats twelve cities for those remaining Levites.

relationship: Town-and-surrounding-land gift under the Mosaic instruction
rationale: Both describe Israel supplying Levites with towns and surrounding lands, with Numbers explicitly stating dwelling and livestock uses and Joshua describing the commanded distribution by lot.

relationship: Same-chapter donating tribes and Aaronic allocation header
rationale: Judah, Simeon and some of Benjamin supply the cities, matching the three tribal sources already named for Aaron's thirteen-city Kohathite allotment.

relationship: Same-chapter Aaron's Kohathite recipients identified in the lot summary
rationale: The cities are assigned to Aaron's Kohathite family, corresponding to the earlier header naming Aaron's priests among Kohath's division and their thirteen-city lot.

relationship: Hebron's explicit Arbok and Anakim description repeated
rationale: Both explicitly identify the city of Arbok as Hebron and call it the Anakim's mother-city, preserving the source's own identification rather than adding a modern site claim.

relationship: Caleb's Hebron possession and its specified fields and villages
rationale: The earlier grant identifies Hebron as Caleb's lot; this allocation specifies the city's fields and villages for Caleb's sons alongside the priestly city account, without harmonizing every land term.

relationship: Hebron's Levitical grant and refuge appointment
rationale: The Aaronic grant expressly calls Hebron a refuge for the killer, corresponding to the earlier refuge appointment of Arbok-Hebron in Judah's mountain.

relationship: Same-chapter Ailom-Tema entries within the nine-city subgroup
rationale: Ailom and Tema contribute to the Aaronic subgroup that closes at Bethsamys with nine cities from the two stated tribes, retaining these supplied name forms.

relationship: Same-chapter Gella-Debir entries and subgroup total
rationale: Gella and Debir form part of the same Aaronic list whose following closure counts nine cities from the two tribes; their allotted lands are retained separately.

relationship: Same-chapter nine-city subtotal and its preceding six names
rationale: Asa, Tany and Bethsamys complete the stated nine-city group after Hebron, Libnah, Ailom, Tema, Gella and Debir, without renaming the entries to another edition.

relationship: Same-chapter first Benjamin pair and four-city subtotal
rationale: Gibeon and Gathet begin Benjamin's Aaronic contribution; Anathoth and Gamala complete the following pair and explicit four-city subtotal.

relationship: Same-chapter Benjamin subtotal completed from the preceding pair
rationale: Anathoth and Gamala complete the four-city Benjamin group begun by Gibeon and Gathet, each retaining its allotted lands and own source anchor.

relationship: Same-chapter thirteen Aaronic cities through nine-plus-four subtotals
rationale: The thirteen-city Aaronic total follows the stated nine-city two-tribe subgroup and four-city Benjamin subgroup, connecting the actual subtotals without altering their names.

relationship: Same-chapter Ephraim segment within remaining Kohath's lot
rationale: The remaining Kohathite divisions begin receiving cities from Ephraim, one of the three contributors named in their ten-city allotment header.

relationship: Shechem in Ephraim as refuge and Levitical city
rationale: Both explicitly identify Shechem as a refuge in Ephraim's mountain or portion, while the Levitical grant also includes Gazara and allotted lands.

relationship: Same-chapter four-city Ephraim subtotal and its initial pair
rationale: Kabsaïm and Upper Beth-horon close the four-city Ephraim contribution after Shechem and Gazara, within the remaining Kohathite portion described in the preceding units.

relationship: Same-chapter Dan's two pairs and four-city contribution
rationale: Elkothaim and Gethedan introduce Dan's contribution; Aijalon and Gath-rimmon complete it with the explicit four-city count, preserving every allotted-land entry.

relationship: Same-chapter Dan subtotal completed by two named pairs
rationale: Aijalon and Gath-rimmon finish the four-city group begun with Elkothaim and Gethedan from Dan, retaining the original forms rather than harmonizing spellings.

relationship: Same-chapter two Manassite cities within Kohath's ten-city total
rationale: Taanach and Jebatha are explicitly two cities from half-Manasseh, completing the contributions summarized as ten cities for the remaining Kohathite divisions.

relationship: Same-chapter Kohathite total and four-four-two tribal subtotals
rationale: The ten-city total follows four from Ephraim, four from Dan and two from half-Manasseh, preserving the catalogue's own counts and recipient division.

relationship: Gaulon in Bashan as Manassite refuge and Gershonite grant
rationale: Gaulon in Bashan occurs in both Manasseh's eastern refuge appointment and its Gershonite contribution; Bosora here is not conflated with Reuben's differently placed Bosor.

relationship: Same-chapter Issachar's initial Gershonite pair and subtotal
rationale: Kison and Debba begin the Issachar contribution, followed by Remmath and Spring of Letters and the four-city subtotal, retaining the named land grants.

relationship: Same-chapter Issachar four-city group completed from its first pair
rationale: Remmath and Spring of Letters complete the Issachar contribution begun with Kison and Debba, preserving the explicit four-city total and original names.

relationship: Same-chapter Asher's paired entries and four-city contribution
rationale: Basellan and Dabbon introduce Asher's Gershonite towns; Helkath and Rehob supply the concluding pair and four-city subtotal in the next unit.

relationship: Same-chapter Asher four-city group and preceding named pair
rationale: Helkath and Rehob complete the Asher group begun by Basellan and Dabbon, connecting the exact listed towns to their four-city total.

relationship: Kedesh in Galilee as Naphtali's refuge and Levitical contribution
rationale: Both explicitly name Kedesh in Galilee as a refuge within Naphtali, while the Gershonite grant adds Emmath and Themmon to form three cities.

relationship: Same-chapter Gershon's closing total and allocation header
rationale: The Gershonite closure repeats the thirteen-city total introduced in its lot from Manasseh, Issachar, Asher and Naphtali, without changing the underlying town entries.

relationship: Same-chapter Zebulun's first Merarite pair and four-city subtotal
rationale: Maan and Kedesh begin Zebulun's Merarite contribution; Dimnah and Sella complete the following four-city total, without identifying this Kedesh as Naphtali's refuge.

relationship: Same-chapter Zebulun contribution completed by its second pair
rationale: Dimnah and Sella finish the four-city Zebulun group begun with Maan and Kedesh, preserving this particular tribe and Levitical division.

relationship: Bosor in Reuben as refuge and Merarite grant
rationale: Both explicitly identify Bosor as Reuben's eastern wilderness refuge; the Merarite grant also names Jazer, kept distinct from the later Gad entry with that name.

relationship: Same-chapter Reuben four-city subtotal and initial refuge pair
rationale: Dekmon and Mapha complete Reuben's four-city contribution after Bosor and Jazer, with Bosor's refuge description retained and no duplicate-name suppression.

relationship: Ramoth in Gad's Gilead named as a refuge
rationale: Both name Ramoth in Gilead for Gad, with Joshua explicitly granting its refuge city and lands to Merari alongside Kamin, without silently replacing Aremoth elsewhere.

relationship: Same-chapter Gad's four-city group completed after its refuge pair
rationale: Heshbon and Jazer complete Gad's four cities after Ramoth and Kamin, keeping this Jazer entry separate from the Reuben contribution.

relationship: Same-chapter Merari's closing total and three-tribe allotment header
rationale: The Merarite closure repeats twelve cities, corresponding to the lot introduced from Reuben, Gad and Zebulun, with its actual constituent entries preserved.

relationship: Forty-eight Levitical towns commanded and totaled
rationale: Numbers commands forty-eight towns with their outlying lands; Joshua totals forty-eight Levitical cities with surrounding lands within Israel's possessions.

relationship: Surrounding lands attached to every Levitical city
rationale: Both attach surrounding land to the Levitical towns; Numbers gives dwelling, livestock and measurements, while Joshua emphasizes that the arrangement applies to every listed city.

relationship: Completion of division repeated after the allotment closure
rationale: The continuation says Joshua finished dividing the land, corresponding to the earlier closing account of completed tribal lots distributed by Joshua, Eleazar and ancestral leaders.

relationship: Repeated grant of Joshua's requested Ephraim city
rationale: Both record Israel granting Joshua a portion by command and identify his requested city as Thamnasarach in Ephraim's mountain, preserving its supplied name.

relationship: Repeated building and dwelling after the requested grant
rationale: Both state that Joshua built the city and lived in it, following the grant of his requested Thamnasarach portion in Ephraim.

relationship: Circumcision stone knives and their later preservation
rationale: The continuation preserves the knives used for circumcision in Thamnasarach; the earlier narrative records the command to make stone knives and Joshua making and using them.

relationship: Promised land inheritance and narrated possession
rationale: Deuteronomy announces crossing Jordan to inherit and dwell in the given land; Joshua states that the Lord gave the sworn land and Israel inherited and lived there.

relationship: Promised surrounding rest and narrated enemy delivery
rationale: Both describe rest from surrounding enemies in the inherited land, with Joshua explicitly presenting the rest and enemy delivery as fulfillment of the fathers' oath.

relationship: Repeated statement that no divine good word failed
rationale: Both assert that none of the Lord's spoken good words proved untrue, with the farewell exhortation calling Israel to acknowledge this in heart and soul.

relationship: The same three eastern tribal groups addressed
rationale: Joshua summons Reuben, Gad and half-Manasseh, the same groups addressed at the beginning concerning their land and duty to assist their brothers.

relationship: Promised obedience and later commendation
rationale: The tribes initially pledge to obey Joshua as Moses; Joshua now commends their heeding both leaders, preserving the different speakers and stages of the exchange.

relationship: Continued support of brothers under the earlier condition
rationale: Joshua commends their not forsaking their brothers, corresponding to the command to cross equipped and fight alongside them until those brothers receive rest.

relationship: Return home permitted after the brothers receive rest
rationale: Both connect return to the eastern inheritance with the Lord giving rest to the other brothers; Joshua announces that the condition for return has now been met.

relationship: Love, walking, command keeping and wholehearted service
rationale: Both combine love, walking in the Lord's ways and command keeping with wholehearted service; Joshua says mind and soul and adds clinging, while Deuteronomy says heart and soul.

relationship: Narrated dismissal follows the earlier promised return
rationale: Joshua blesses and sends the eastern tribes home, corresponding to his initial instruction that each would return to the Mosaic inheritance when the brothers had rest.

relationship: Bashan inheritance assigned to half-Manasseh
rationale: Both identify Moses' eastern Bashan grant to half-Manasseh; Joshua additionally distinguishes the other half's western inheritance, without conflating the two portions.

relationship: Related enemy-spoil distributions with distinct recipient descriptions
rationale: Both describe enemy spoil being shared; Numbers specifies warriors and the whole congregation, while Joshua says the eastern tribes divided it with their brothers and gives no distribution proportions.

relationship: Eastern tribes' Mosaic possession and their return
rationale: Both identify Gad, Reuben and half-Manasseh as recipients of Moses' eastern inheritance; Joshua22 narrates departure from Shiloh for that Gilead possession.

relationship: Same-chapter visible altar construction and its declared testimonial purpose
rationale: The large Jordan-side altar initially reported is later explained by its builders as a generational testimony, explicitly not an altar intended for offerings or sacrifices.

relationship: Same-chapter construction and the report that triggers alarm
rationale: The report concerns the altar just built by the three eastern groups beside Jordan, preserving Galgala and the report's Gilead wording without geographical harmonization.

relationship: Same-chapter proposed war reversed after the report is heard
rationale: Israel first gathers at Shiloh for war; after the delegation's report, the people bless God and decide not to destroy the eastern tribes' land.

relationship: Phinehas' genealogy and earlier Peor intervention
rationale: The envoy is Phinehas son of Eleazar son of Aaron, the same named priestly line in the earlier Peor intervention, which the delegation subsequently recalls.

relationship: Same-chapter ten leaders accompanying the named priestly envoy
rationale: The ten ancestral leaders accompany Phinehas in the mission to the eastern tribes, retaining their stated one-per-tribe selection and commanders-of-thousands role without deriving a new tribal total.

relationship: Same-chapter delegation's arrival and specified accusation
rationale: The delegates arrive among Gad, Reuben and half-Manasseh and deliver the following altar accusation, supported in their speech by the Peor and Achar examples.

relationship: Altar accusation against the background of restricted offering location
rationale: The delegation alleges departure through a separate altar; Deuteronomy restricts burnt offerings to the chosen place, while the later response denies that this altar is for sacrifice.

relationship: Explicit Peor-plague recollection and its narrative
rationale: The delegation recalls Peor's sin and plague upon the congregation; Numbers describes Baal-of-Peor worship, divine anger and the plague stopped after Phinehas' intervention.

relationship: Same-chapter predicted communal wrath and the individual-offense example
rationale: The warning that eastern apostasy would bring wrath upon all Israel is illustrated by Achar's single devoted-property offense bringing wrath beyond himself.

relationship: Single authorized offering place in a conditional relocation appeal
rationale: The delegation offers shared land if the eastern possession is too small and rejects a separate sacrificial altar; Deuteronomy likewise restricts burnt offerings to the chosen place.

relationship: Achar's devoted-property offense and collective losses
rationale: Both link Achar's devoted-property offense with communal wrath; Joshua7 narrates about thirty-six killed and gives Carmi and Zambri between Achar and Zerah, preserving the differing ancestry formulations.

relationship: Same-chapter reply introduced and its opening conditional declaration
rationale: The eastern tribes answer the commanders with an appeal to God's knowledge and conditional accountability if their altar was built in apostasy or for sacrifice.

relationship: Same-chapter appeal to divine knowledge and explanation of intention
rationale: The appeal that God knows their purpose is developed by rejecting sacrificial rebellion and explaining the children's future exclusion concern and testimonial altar.

relationship: Same-chapter sacrificial-purpose condition answered by its explicit denial
rationale: The tribes accept accountability if their altar is for offerings, then state that it is not for offerings but a testimony against future denial of their portion.

relationship: Same-chapter future-child concern and the proposed testimony
rationale: The concern about future children questioning their connection to Israel's God develops into the imagined Jordan-boundary exclusion and the altar's proposed generational witness.

relationship: Same-chapter feared denial of a portion and testimonial response
rationale: The imagined claim that the Jordan leaves them no portion in the Lord is answered by a model altar intended to prevent that denial to later generations.

relationship: Same-chapter rejected sacrificial use and positively stated purpose
rationale: The decision to build an altar not for offerings or sacrifices is followed by its positive role as testimony for shared service and future generations.

relationship: Same-chapter shared-service testimony responds to the imagined exclusion
rationale: The altar's testimony to a shared portion and service answers the previously imagined children's claim that the Jordan separates the eastern descendants from the Lord.

relationship: Same-chapter repeated denial of sacrificial use
rationale: The description of an altar likeness as testimony repeats the earlier statement that the constructed altar is not for offerings or sacrifices.

relationship: Denied separate sacrificial altar and restricted offering location
rationale: The tribes deny departing by offering away from the Lord's altar before His tent; Deuteronomy prohibits burnt offerings at arbitrary places and requires the chosen place.

relationship: Same-chapter pleased reception and explicit no-offense verdict
rationale: The priest and leaders hear the eastern explanation with pleasure, after which Phinehas states that no offense was committed and Israel was delivered from the Lord's hand.

relationship: Same-chapter no-offense verdict after the stated testimonial defense
rationale: Phinehas' favorable verdict follows the explicit non-sacrificial testimony explanation and rejection of offering apart from the Lord's altar before His tent, without turning the initial allegation into a finding.

relationship: Same-chapter delegation's report and the congregation's response
rationale: Phinehas and the leaders return from Gilead and report the words; the congregation accepts them, blesses God and abandons the proposed war.

relationship: Same-chapter abandoned war contrasted with the initial mobilization
rationale: The decision not to attack or destroy the eastern land reverses Israel's earlier gathering at Shiloh for war, following the heard and accepted explanation.

relationship: Same-chapter Joshua's testimony declaration and the builders' stated purpose
rationale: Joshua calls the altar a testimony that the Lord is their God, corresponding to its builders' generational-witness explanation; no unprovided altar name is substituted.

relationship: Repeated description of Joshua's advanced age
rationale: Both describe Joshua as old and advanced in days, while chapter13 introduces remaining land and chapter23 introduces the farewell after surrounding rest.

relationship: Related Joshua assemblies of Israel's leaders
rationale: Both describe Joshua summoning Israel with elders, scribes and judges; chapter23 emphasizes his age, while chapter24 explicitly locates the assembly at Shiloh before God.

relationship: Divine fighting recalled and narrated in the Amorite campaign
rationale: The farewell attributes the nations' defeat to the Lord fighting for Israel; the Gibeon account likewise expressly says the Lord fought alongside Israel.

relationship: Remaining peoples assigned by lot within the Jordan-to-sea extent
rationale: Both combine remaining inhabitants with distributing land by lots and describe the Jordan-to-Great-Sea span, preserving allocation language alongside incomplete occupation.

relationship: Promised removal of opposing nations and their kings
rationale: Both promise divine action destroying opposing nations and kings before Israel; Joshua additionally names wild beasts as an agent, a detail not supplied by the Deuteronomy target.

relationship: Repeated law observance without right-or-left deviation
rationale: Both urge strength in keeping Moses' commands and prohibit turning right or left, with the farewell expressly identifying the written law book.

relationship: Prohibition on naming the remaining nations' gods
rationale: Both forbid uttering other gods' names; Joshua additionally prohibits bowing and service and applies the warning to the nations remaining among the hearers.

relationship: Repeated command to cling to the Lord
rationale: Both expressly command clinging or cleaving to the Lord, with Deuteronomy also naming fear, service and swearing by His name.

relationship: Stronger nations overcome and no opponent withstanding
rationale: Deuteronomy promises removal of stronger nations and none standing before Israel; Joshua declares that great strong nations were destroyed and none has stood against them.

relationship: One pursuing a thousand under different descriptions of divine agency
rationale: Both use one pursuing a thousand; Joshua credits the Lord fighting for Israel, whereas Deuteronomy's rhetorical question uses God's selling and handing-over language without assigning its pronouns a new referent.

relationship: Love for the Lord in repeated covenant instruction
rationale: Joshua commands careful love for the Lord, corresponding to the command of love with the whole heart, soul and strength in Moses' instruction.

relationship: Intermarriage warning within threatened religious defection
rationale: Both warn against marriages with the remaining nations; Deuteronomy expressly describes sons being turned toward other gods, while Joshua's following warning describes the resulting snares.

relationship: Remaining inhabitants as bodily irritants and enemies
rationale: Both describe unremoved inhabitants through sharp bodily imagery; Joshua names nails in heels and darts in eyes, while Numbers names eye splinters and missiles in sides.

relationship: Repeated assurance that no divine good word failed
rationale: Both state that none of the Lord's good words proved false; Joshua's farewell calls the hearers to recognize this in their heart and soul.

relationship: Good received followed by threatened destruction from the land
rationale: Both place experienced divine good beside threatened destruction and removal from the given land, preserving the farewell's future harmful words and Deuteronomy's rejoicing language.

relationship: Other-god service followed by covenant destruction
rationale: Both warn that forsaking the Lord for serving and bowing to other gods brings destruction, with Joshua explicitly identifying the act as covenant transgression.

relationship: Israel assembled before God at Shiloh
rationale: Both locate the gathering at Shiloh; chapter18 places the Tabernacle there, while chapter24 names elders, scribes and judges standing before God.

relationship: Terah's family and the pre-Canaan ancestral residence
rationale: Both identify Terah as father of Abraham or Abram and Nahor; Genesis describes their Chaldean and Harran setting, while Joshua additionally states the fathers' other-god service.

relationship: Abraham's departure and movement through the promised land
rationale: Genesis narrates the divine call from the father's house and Abram's travel from Harran through Canaan; Joshua summarizes the Lord taking and leading Abraham from beyond the River.

relationship: Isaac given to Abraham in recap and birth account
rationale: Joshua's recital names Isaac as the son given Abraham; Genesis describes Sarah bearing him according to the Lord's word and Abraham naming him Isaac.

relationship: Jacob and Esau given to Isaac
rationale: The recap names Isaac's sons Jacob and Esau; Genesis narrates their twin birth and naming, without importing the rest of Joshua's Seir and Egypt recital into that passage.

relationship: Esau's Seir possession attributed to divine gift
rationale: Both explicitly describe Mount Seir as a possession given to Esau or his sons, while Deuteronomy uses this to prohibit Israel taking their land.

relationship: Jacob and his descendants enter Egypt
rationale: Both state that Jacob and his sons went into Egypt; Genesis additionally enumerates the descendants and possessions brought, while Joshua adds their subsequent growth.

relationship: Egypt struck before Israel's departure
rationale: The recital connects divine blows against Egypt with departure; Exodus describes the firstborn judgment and Pharaoh's ensuing command for Israel to leave, without claiming this exhausts all the blows.

relationship: Israel enters the sea and Egyptian chariots pursue
rationale: Both describe Israel entering the sea and Egyptians following with horses and chariots; Exodus additionally describes dry ground and water walls for Israel.

relationship: Cloud-darkness separation and sea covering the pursuers
rationale: Both describe a cloud and darkness separating the camps before the sea covers Egypt's force; Exodus supplies the successive movements and Moses' stretched-out hand.

relationship: Eastern Amorite land taken before the Jordan crossing
rationale: Both describe possession taken from Amorite rulers beyond Jordan; Deuteronomy specifies two kings and the Arnon-to-Hermon extent, while Joshua summarizes their battle and defeat.

relationship: Balak summons Balaam to curse Israel
rationale: Both identify Balak son of Zippor as Moab's king who summons Balaam for a curse; Numbers supplies the envoys, fear and requested military advantage.

relationship: Divine refusal of destruction and curse reversed into blessing
rationale: Both describe the Lord preserving Israel and blessing despite the curse sought through Balaam; Deuteronomy expressly says He refused Balaam and changed the curse because of His love.

relationship: Jericho's resistance and divine delivery
rationale: The recital says Jericho's inhabitants opposed Israel and were delivered to them; the earlier account describes Jericho fortified and the Lord announcing its delivery before the wall-fall instruction.

relationship: Insects sent before Israel to drive out opponents
rationale: Both attribute displacement to divinely sent insects; Joshua says wasps and twelve Amorite kings, while Exodus says hornets and names four peoples, preserving the differing descriptions.

relationship: Received cities and crops not produced by Israel
rationale: Both describe cities Israel did not build and vineyards and olive groves it did not plant, with Joshua presenting the settled gift and Deuteronomy announcing it beforehand.

relationship: Foreign gods to be removed from the community
rationale: Joshua commands removal of the fathers' foreign gods and faithful service; Jacob similarly commands his household to put away foreign gods, without equating their separate gatherings.

relationship: Same-chapter choice of service answered by the community's pledge
rationale: Joshua presents alternatives and his household's allegiance; the later reply pledges the Lord's service and is acknowledged as the people's own chosen witness.

relationship: Same-chapter refusal to abandon the Lord and stated historical reasons
rationale: The people reject serving other gods and explain their response through the Lord's Egyptian deliverance, protection on the road and removal of the land's nations.

relationship: Same-chapter community recollection of the recital's deliverance and journey
rationale: The people's appeal to deliverance and protection recalls the earlier sea rescue, wilderness journey and eastern Amorite defeat in Joshua's speech, preserving their different speakers.

relationship: Same-chapter removed nations in the people's response and prior recital
rationale: The people's promise to serve their God follows their recollection of driven-out Amorites and other nations, corresponding to the preceding eastern and western conquest recital.

relationship: Jealous divine character within warnings against rival service
rationale: Both describe the Lord as jealous and connect other-god worship with judgment; Joshua's severe warning concerning forgiveness is retained without replacing it with Exodus' generational formulation.

relationship: Forsaking the Lord for other gods brings threatened consumption
rationale: Both warn against abandoning the Lord to serve other gods and announce destruction; Joshua explicitly contrasts the threatened affliction with the good already received.

relationship: Same-chapter stated service pledge acknowledged as the people's choice
rationale: The people's repeated insistence that they will serve the Lord is answered by Joshua declaring them witnesses that they have chosen His service.

relationship: People's choice of the Lord for service and obedience
rationale: Both expressly describe choosing the Lord as their God or for His service, with Deuteronomy additionally naming walking, ordinances, judgments and hearing His voice.

relationship: Repeated command to remove present foreign gods
rationale: Both command putting away foreign gods from among the addressed community; Joshua additionally directs their heart to Israel's God, while Jacob adds purification and changed garments.

relationship: Pledged service and obedience to the chosen God's voice
rationale: The people pledge service and hearing the Lord's voice, corresponding to the earlier covenant declaration of choosing God and hearkening to Him with obedient conduct.

relationship: Covenant-making associated with delivered law and judgment
rationale: Joshua gives law and judgment in a Shiloh covenant; Exodus describes Moses delivering words and ordinances and making the covenant with book and blood, preserving the different ceremonies.

relationship: Written law records preserved as covenant testimony
rationale: Joshua writes the words in a scroll of God's law; Moses completes the law book and orders its placement by the ark as witness, while Joshua also erects a stone.

relationship: Same-chapter erected stone and its expressly assigned testimony
rationale: Joshua's speech assigns testimonial hearing and future witness to the great stone just set beneath the terebinth, retaining the text's own description without archaeological verification.

relationship: Closely repeated dismissal to personal inheritances
rationale: Both describe Joshua sending the people away and each going to his own place, house or inheritance, with Judges explicitly naming possession of the land.

relationship: Repeated period of service under Joshua and surviving elders
rationale: Both state that Israel served the Lord through Joshua's days and those of the elders who outlived him and knew or saw the Lord's works.

relationship: Repeated death age and servant designation
rationale: Both identify Joshua son of Nun as the Lord's servant and state that he died at one hundred ten years, retaining the same named subject and age.

relationship: Burial accounts sharing Ephraim and north-of-Gaash details
rationale: Both place Joshua's burial in his inheritance in Ephraim's mountain north of Gaash; Thamnathasachara and Timnath-heres remain in their supplied forms without independent name identification.

relationship: Buried circumcision knives and their earlier commanded making
rationale: The continuation places the stone circumcision knives in Joshua's tomb; the earlier narrative records the command to make sharp stone knives and Joshua making and using them.

relationship: Joseph's bones carried from Egypt and finally buried
rationale: Joshua records the bones brought up from Egypt and buried at Shechem; Exodus expressly describes Moses taking those bones in fulfillment of Joseph's oath instruction.

relationship: Shechem field purchase with preserved seller and price wording
rationale: Both describe Jacob acquiring a Shechem field for a hundred lambs; Joshua says ewe lambs and Amorite inhabitants, while Genesis names Hamor father of Shechem, without harmonizing those descriptions.

relationship: Same-chapter Eleazar's death and Phinehas' subsequent priestly service
rationale: Eleazar dies and is buried at his son's Gabaath; the continuation records Phinehas succeeding him and eventually being buried at his own Gabaath, preserving both notices.

relationship: Phinehas' priestly line and covenant before his succession
rationale: The continuation names Phinehas succeeding Eleazar; Numbers identifies him as Eleazar's son in Aaron's line and grants him and his seed an enduring priesthood covenant.

relationship: Other-god service followed by delivery to enemies
rationale: Both connect serving other gods with the Lord handing Israel to enemies; Joshua names Astarte, Ashtaroth and Eglom, while Judges names Baal and Astartes with a broader enemy description.

relationship: Moabite ruler's eighteen-year dominion in distinct narrative placements
rationale: Both record eighteen years under Moab's ruler after Israel's evil; the names Eglom and Eglon and the different placement of the notices are preserved without chronology harmonization.
